gold.abstract: Participation incentives is a well-known issue inhibiting randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in medicine, as well as a potential cause of user dissatisfaction for RCTs in online platforms. We frame this issue as a non-standard exploration-exploitation tradeoff: an RCT would like to explore as uniformly as possible, whereas each "agent" (a patient or a user) prefers "exploitation", i.e., treatments that seem best. We incentivize participation by leveraging information asymmetry between the trial and the agents. We measure statistical performance via worst-case estimation error under adversarially generated outcomes, a standard objective for RCTs. We obtain a near-optimal solution in terms of this objective: an incentive-compatible mechanism with a particular guarantee, and a nearly matching impossibility result for any incentive-compatible mechanism. We consider three model variants: homogeneous agents (of the same "type" comprising beliefs and preferences), heterogeneous agents, and an extension that leverages estimated type frequencies to mitigate the influence of rare-but-difficult agent types.

These are your colleagues' latest proposals:

--- Researcher B ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper-b reviews adaptive clinical trial designs, distinguishing prospective, concurrent (ad hoc), and retrospective adaptations, and warns that unplanned modifications may alter the patient population and inflate type I error.  
Paper-c provides conjoint-analysis utilities from 108 Alzheimer’s disease study partners, showing home visits (utility 0.89) can offset high intervention risk disutility (-0.85), while car service adds little; predicted participation rises from 17% to 27% with amenities and to 60% with higher active-treatment chance.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
Conjoint-derived utilities become quantitative enrollment/retention weights inside a prospective adaptive design. Preference data do not merely describe willingness; they operationally drive pre-specified adaptation rules—e.g., add home visits if enrollment falls below a threshold—while keeping the adaptation prospective to control type I error.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
Stage 1: administer a conjoint survey to 200 AD study partners, adding adaptive-design attributes (interim analysis frequency, sample-size re-estimation) to paper-c’s risk, home visit, transport, and active-treatment attributes. Estimate utilities.  
Stage 2: build trial simulations where enrollment/retention are functions of those utilities. Compare fixed, standard adaptive, and preference-weighted adaptive designs. Measure type I error under null scenarios, power, time to full enrollment, and retention. Validate by benchmarking predicted participation against paper-c’s 27% amenity increase and against a pilot AD trial recruitment dataset.  
Missing cross-paper knowledge: neither paper measures preferences for adaptive features nor links preference utilities to statistical operating characteristics; new conjoint and simulation data are required.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
We propose preference-weighted adaptive designs that use AD study partners’ conjoint utilities for trial attributes to pre-specify adaptation rules, aiming to improve recruitment and retention without inflating type I error. Simulations and a pilot validation will test whether preference-informed adaptations outperform standard adaptive and fixed designs.

FINAL IDEA: Integrating conjoint-derived participant preferences into prospective adaptive trial rules can jointly optimize recruitment, retention, and statistical validity.

--- Researcher C ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper-b reviews adaptive trial designs, distinguishing prospective, concurrent, and retrospective adaptations, and warns that post-adaptation changes can shift the enrolled population from the target population and inflate type I error. Paper-c provides conjoint-analysis utilities from 108 AD study partners: home visits had highest utility (0.89), offsetting high-risk disutility (−0.85); car service added little; utility varied with patient severity.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
I propose that preference utilities from paper-c can serve as retention weights in paper-b’s prospective adaptation rule. If an adaptation changes visit burden, transport, or risk, its predicted effect on study-partner willingness can be used to select adaptations that reduce non-random dropout and keep the accrued sample closer to the target population.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
First, extend paper-c’s conjoint experiment to include adaptive attributes, such as mid-trial switch to home visits, added transport, or changed visit frequency, and estimate utilities in a new AD study-partner sample. Second, build a prospective adaptive trial simulation using paper-b’s framework. At interim analyses, candidate adaptations are selected by a composite score: statistical promise plus predicted preference utility, constrained by target-population representativeness. Compare preference-blind adaptation, preference-weighted adaptation, and no adaptation. Measure type I error, population drift, retention, and duration; validate with bootstrap and sensitivity analysis. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no available source directly tests whether mid-trial adaptations change willingness or whether preference-weighting reduces drift; this is a proposed hypothesis.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
Adaptive trials can drift from the target population when mid-trial changes alter burden or risk. This project embeds study-partner preference utilities, estimated by conjoint analysis, into prospective adaptation rules for AD trials. Simulation will test whether preference-weighted adaptations improve retention and representativeness without inflating type I error.

FINAL IDEA: Adaptive clinical trial designs should incorporate conjoint-estimated participant/study-partner preferences as retention weights in adaptation rules to reduce population drift and preserve validity.
